planting.note: Divide and repot into a wide basket once new growths outgrow the container, ideally as fresh roots emerge in spring.

directions: Named for its near-black, waxy lip marked with jet ridges set against apple-green sepals and petals, this Bornean and Malaysian species produces pendant racemes of several fragrant blooms from the base of each new pseudobulb. It scrambles horizontally, so it is best grown in a wide basket or on a raft rather than a standard pot, where its rambling rhizome can spread unchecked. Bright filtered light, high humidity, and a distinct cooler, drier rest after growths mature help trigger the heavy spring flush of bloom. The rambling habit and dark lip distinguish it instantly from the more compact, white-flowered Coelogyne cristata already common in cultivation.

planting.note: Repot or divide clumps in spring right as new growths begin, since the pendant flower spikes emerge from the base of immature growths and should not be disturbed once forming.

directions: A Himalayan-foothill species bearing arching to pendulous racemes of cream to pale straw flowers, each lip painted with rusty-orange markings, produced in loose chains that can hold a dozen or more blooms. Because spikes hang downward from the base of new growths, it is usually mounted or grown in a basket to let the inflorescence drape freely below the foliage. It prefers intermediate temperatures, bright indirect light, and a cooler, slightly drier winter rest after the pseudobulbs mature to encourage reliable late-winter flowering. The looser habit and orange-blotched lip separate it from the tighter, snow-white blooms of the far more common Coelogyne cristata.

planting.note: Repot into a shallow, well-drained pot in spring after flowering, since this species resents frequent root disturbance and blooms best when slightly potbound.

directions: A Vietnamese species prized for upright racemes of pure white flowers centered by a golden-orange-marked lip, often called the bride orchid for its clean, luminous coloring and lightly ruffled lip margin. Unlike many pendulous-flowered Coelogyne, its spikes stand upright above the foliage, making it a favorite for display and for cut flowers. It grows best in bright, filtered light with intermediate temperatures and steady moisture during active growth, tapering off in winter once pseudobulbs mature. The upright white blooms with a bold orange throat readily distinguish it from both the pendant chains of Coelogyne flaccida and the crested, coral-marked lip of Coelogyne cristata.

planting.note: Mount or pot in an open, fast-draining mix in spring, since this lowland species dislikes soggy roots but wants near-constant humidity year round.

directions: A warm-growing Indonesian species with short, almost stemless pseudobulbs and unusually large single flowers in olive-green to rusty-brown tones, the fringed, dark maroon-striped lip protruding dramatically forward of the sepals. Its low, clustering growth habit and near-continuous, sequential blooming through the year set it apart from the seasonal flushes typical of most Coelogyne species. It thrives mounted or in a shallow basket with year-round warmth, high humidity, and bright but filtered light, never drying out completely between waterings. The shaggy, protruding lip and somber earth-toned coloring make it one of the more unusual-looking members of the genus rather than a showy white- or cream-flowered type.

planting.note: Mount on bark or a small slab in spring, since the creeping rhizome and small pseudobulbs establish fastest with open airflow around the roots.

directions: A compact Southeast Asian species with small, closely spaced pseudobulbs along a creeping rhizome, each topped by a single leaf and, in season, short umbels of small cream to yellow flowers finely speckled and streaked with maroon spots. The delicate mottled pattern on the twisting petals gives the species its painted common name and makes it a favorite miniature for mounted collections. It prefers bright, filtered light, constant humidity, and year-round warmth with no true dry rest, drying only briefly between waterings. Its diminutive size and spotted, twisted floral segments distinguish it readily from the far larger, strap-leaved Bulbophyllum lobbii or the pendant, medusa-like Bulbophyllum medusae already grown widely.

planting.note: Mount or pot in a shallow, airy basket in spring, since the fine hair-tipped petals and delicate flowers are easily damaged by handling once buds begin to swell.

directions: A Southeast Asian miniature closely related to the fringed slipper-orchid-mimicking Bulbophyllum group, producing solitary deep maroon-purple flowers with long, fine, hair-like appendages fringing the lateral petals that quiver in the slightest air movement to attract pollinating flies. Each bloom emerges low among the small clustered pseudobulbs, giving the appearance of the flower resting directly on the potting medium. It grows best in intermediate to warm temperatures with high humidity, bright filtered light, and a brief drying period between waterings rather than a hard seasonal rest. The single large maroon bloom fringed with quivering hairs is unmistakable next to the tiny globose flowers of Bulbophyllum medusae or the giant blooms of Bulbophyllum phalaenopsis.

planting.note: Repot into fresh bark mix in spring after flowering as new growth begins, giving roots time to establish before the next bloom cycle.

directions: One of the most famous Hawaiian-bred orchid hybrids, this cross between the night-fragrant Brassavola nodosa and a reed-stem Cattleya parent produces clusters of lavender-pink, star-shaped flowers with a broad, ruffled white-and-magenta lip that releases a strong sweet fragrance most noticeably in the evening. Long grown commercially for cut flowers and Hawaiian lei-making, it flowers repeatedly through the year on a compact, upright plant rather than on the single seasonal flush typical of many Cattleya-alliance orchids. It wants bright light approaching full sun, warm temperatures, and a well-drained bark mix that dries somewhat between waterings. The strongly star-shaped flower form and heavy evening fragrance, inherited from its Brassavola parent, set it apart from rounder-flowered standard Cattleya hybrids.
